name: Karl Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I accompany a civic choir at the piano, record rehearsal guides and coach two singers on their parts. I earned a bachelor’s degree in music and have played for pay for twenty-five years. I can hold a room together when the choir rushes, though the paid hours on my sheet keep getting shorter.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home when the choir season slows?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, my grown children live elsewhere, and my partner works irregular shifts at a print counter. We rent and have two weeks of expenses saved. My musician pay is below usual, and there are few accompanist posts close enough to reach by bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the choir that a faster rehearsal notice helps if the pianist’s paid hours are still attached. A reminder cannot play the entrance for a singer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two weeks saved and my partner’s uneven counter shifts make a late choir cheque frightening already. Small AI gains do not change how close rent comes after a quiet month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep paid choir rehearsals, guide recordings and two singing clients, and request written pay dates from the choir office. In the first year of this modest change, I would keep using AI daily for drafts of rehearsal lists, but check names and timings against the conductor’s marked score before sending anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the next thin month, even if AI barely changes my job. The rent date does not move with the concert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How late has a cheque been?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The spring concert fee arrived eleven days after rent was due. I borrowed from the grocery envelope and paid it back only after a wedding service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the choir over another delay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need its paid hours first. I would show the office the date and ask for a written pay schedule, not walk away without another offer.

say: I would welcome **faster rehearsal notices** with paid piano hours attached.
I would remind the choir that **a singer’s entrance** still needs my playing.
think: Our **two-week reserve** makes late choir pay a rent problem.
My partner’s **uneven print shifts** offer little cover in a quiet month.
do: Keep **paid choir rehearsals**, guide recordings and two clients.
Request **written pay dates** and check daily AI list drafts against the conductor’s score.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a routine cheque delay reaching rent.
S0.quote: The rent date does not move with the concert.
fieldNote: His **long piano experience** earns below-usual pay on shrinking choir hours.
Daily **AI list drafting** is established use, checked against the marked score before sharing.

steps.text: Keep paid choir rehearsals, rehearsal guides and two singing clients
Request written pay dates and check AI lists against conductor score

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the choir committee that generated guide tracks could replace the recordings it buys from me. I would ask for a written rehearsal rate, including the time spent fixing a singer’s part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those guide tracks bring roughly one-third of my pay. If the committee orders fewer, two weeks saved and a short local job list will not make the gap small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would total guide invoices and ask the choir to pay for an engineer’s lesson outside my paid rehearsal hours on a new AI stem cleaner, a tool that separates voices in a rehearsal recording. In the first year I would try it only on a nameless recording I own, with the choir’s funded licence permitting paid guide use and approved local storage; I would compare every voice by ear with my original and stop if a note shifts or a file leaves the choir system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about a real cut to my guide fees. I like learning software. A cleaned choir-guide file is not a paid booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use a singer’s solo in the test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the trial is on my own singing and piano. A member’s voice needs written permission and a clear storage rule before I would even consider it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays for the engineer’s hour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The choir must pay both the lesson and the licence without taking a paid rehearsal hour from me. If that is unavailable, I keep editing the guide by ear.

say: I would warn **generated guides** may replace paid recording orders.
I would request **written rehearsal rates** that cover time spent fixing parts.
think: Guide tracks provide **one-third of my pay**, leaving little room for a cut.
Two **weeks saved** cannot carry a long search in this town.
do: Count **guide invoices** and request paid engineer instruction outside paid rehearsals this month.
Test **stem cleaner** after paid lesson on owned nameless audio, choir-funded paid-use licence/local storage; compare by ear, stop errors/leakage.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my own guide fees shrinking.
S1.quote: A cleaned choir-guide file is not a paid booking.
fieldNote: His **new AI lesson** differs from daily scheduling use and needs paid time and a funded licence.
The **audio trial** excludes singers’ voices and stops for changed notes or a file leaving approved storage.

steps.text: Count guide invoices and request paid engineer lesson outside paid rehearsals
Test cleaner after paid lesson: owned nameless audio, paid-use licence/local storage; listen, stop errors/leakage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the choir that thinking AGI by 2028 could make rehearsal guides cheaply. Robots able to play piano at rehearsal come around 2031, three years later, so the guide fee faces the first blow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect guide orders to stop in 2028, taking a third of my pay. The live choir may still hire me. Two weeks saved is too little to ride out the loss of my choir-guide fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would total guide invoices, ask for a signed paid choir season and request a real pension estimate before considering a stop at sixty. In the first year after 2028, if paid live hours also fall, I would seek a posted school accompanist job only if my music degree and choir experience meet its requirements, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and bus times fit; I would keep the choir and two clients until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed by an expected loss of a third of my income. The choir hours might hold, but the reserve would be gone fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a school opening now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have seen old adverts, not a current posted paid vacancy. I would ask for written hours and qualifications before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire at sixty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request a real pension estimate first. Two weeks in the bank cannot tell me what a pension might pay.

say: I would distinguish **2028 thinking AGI** from 2031 rehearsal robots.
I would say **guide fees** face the first blow.
think: I expect **guide orders** to end, costing one-third of my pay.
Our **two-week reserve** would vanish quickly during a search.
do: Count **guide invoices**, request a signed paid choir season and an actual pension estimate now.
Seek **posted accompanist work** after 2028 live cuts only if degree/experience qualify, written after-travel net replaces losses and buses fit.
Keep **choir and clients** until a suitable signed offer arrives.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by the likely loss of a third of my pay.
S2.quote: Two weeks saved is too little to ride out the loss of my choir-guide fees.
fieldNote: The **expected 2028 guide loss** comes before 2031 piano-playing robots.
A **school move** needs a real posting, degree/experience fit, replacement net pay and a signed offer.

steps.text: Total guide invoices; request signed paid choir season and actual pension estimate now
Seek posted school role after live cuts if music degree/choir experience qualify and buses fit
Require written after-travel net replacing losses; keep choir/clients until signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the choir that five years until AGI by 2031 gives me time to learn paid venue sound work. Piano-playing robots follow around 2034, after guide recordings change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guides could end by 2031, and the choir might buy fewer rehearsals. I can read a score and follow a sound lead, but I cannot call myself an electrician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I would check that nearby venues accept the certificate for paid assistant work before enrolling in an actual six-month venue-sound training place. I would take it only if the arts centre funds tuition and its paid weekly wages match any choir hours the shifts displace. In the first year after 2031, if guide orders stop and paid choir hours shrink, I would seek a posted sound-assistant job only if the certificate meets its requirements, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and buses fit; I would keep choir and clients until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious until both the course and the job pay. Five years is useful preparation time, but not money in our account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you run live wiring after the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start under a qualified venue electrician and ask for supervised checks. I would not touch live wiring alone before a signed safety sign-off and their approval.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only the tuition is covered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid choir hours and wait for another intake. Free venue-sound tuition with lower weekly income would make rent harder, not easier.

say: I would say **five years** gives time to learn paid venue sound work.
I would put **playing robots** around 2034, after guide-making changes.
think: The **guide fees** may end by 2031, while choir hours could also shrink.
A **sound certificate** helps only if training and later work pay.
do: Take **sound training** only with venue-accepted certificate, funded tuition, real paid place and wages matching displaced choir hours.
Seek **posted sound work** after 2031 guide/choir cuts only if certificate qualifies, after-travel net replaces losses and buses fit.
Keep **choir and clients** until signed offer; work under electrician until live-wiring safety approval.
feel: I feel **anxious** about the gap before any paid new role.
S3.quote: Free venue-sound tuition with lower weekly income would make rent harder, not easier.
fieldNote: The **six-month course** needs venue-recognized certificate, real paid place, funded tuition and no lost weekly choir wages.
The **sound job** requires posted certificate eligibility, after-travel replacement pay and supervised wiring until sign-off.

steps.text: Take sound course only if venues accept certificate, tuition funded, place paid, displaced choir wages matched
Seek posted sound job after guide/choir cuts if certificate qualifies and buses fit
Require written after-travel net replacing losses; keep choir until signed offer
Work under electrician until live-wiring safety sign-off and approval

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that a decade until thinking AGI by 2036 gives us time to check retirement numbers. Piano-playing robots come around 2039. A birthday does not make the rent smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may still need choir and client fees. Two weeks saved today is not evidence that any pension will cover the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would request an actual pension estimate and save fifteen percent of each extra paid wedding-accompaniment fee after rent, food and piano repairs until we have two months of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I would keep paid choir and client work while booked; if live choir hours fall, I would seek a posted school accompanist job only if my degree and experience qualify, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and buses fit. I would keep current work until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still be anxious about paid work at 68, given our short reserve. Ten years lets me check a real pension number, not assume one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if wedding work does not come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I cannot save fifteen percent from it. I will not move grocery money into savings to make the target look reached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your grown children to fill the gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own bills. I would ask them to help read a pension statement, not to pay our rent.

say: I would say **retirement numbers** need checking before 2036.
I would separate **2036 thinking AGI** from 2039 piano-playing robots.
think: At **68**, I may still need choir and client fees.
Two **weeks saved** do not prove a funded retirement.
do: Request **pension estimate** and save 15% of extra paid wedding fees after rent/food/repairs toward two months.
Keep **paid choir and clients** after 2036 while booked and until signed replacement offer.
Seek **posted accompanist work** after live cuts only if degree/experience qualify, after-travel net replaces losses and buses fit.
feel: I feel **anxious** about work at 68 with little saved.
S4.quote: A birthday does not make the rent smaller.
fieldNote: The **pension estimate** is unknown, so his age 68 in 2036 does not prove any retirement entitlement.
The **two-month goal** uses fifteen percent of actual extra wedding fees after rent, food and piano repairs.

steps.text: Request actual pension estimate; keep paid choir/clients after 2036 while booked
Save 15% of extra paid wedding fees after rent/food/repairs toward two months
Seek posted school job after live cuts if music degree/choir experience qualify and buses fit
Require written after-travel net replacing losses; keep paid music until signed offer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the guide fees could stop while only two weeks of bills sit in savings. Signed choir dates, an actual pension estimate, and a posted job with written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how a choir pianist pays rent between seasons. The applause is lovely, but the cheque has to arrive before the landlord does.

headlineQuote: The applause is lovely, but the cheque has to arrive before the landlord does.
portrait: At **58**, Karl is an experienced pianist with a music degree, grown children and only two weeks saved.
His **below-usual pay** comes from choir hours, rehearsal guides and two clients, with few local accompanist posts.
He uses **AI daily** for lists and would learn a new stem cleaner only with paid instruction and controlled audio.
He checks **actual pension income** before slowing down and keeps paid music until a suitable signed replacement offer.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove a third of Karl’s pay while his household has only two weeks saved.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed choir dates**, a real pension estimate and a posted qualified role with written after-travel net pay would help.
